title: Build Route Timer, a slider game where you estimate how long a walk takes
kind: a game chapter: build one game from each pair, and this pair is chapters 17 and 18
one: You build Route Timer in your own project, exactly as it is in Summit Ready, and test it. Then you change it into an estimating game on your own topic.

stages.title: See what Route Timer does and how a round plays

screens.title: Look at a round of Route Timer, from the first leg to the score

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know how a round of Route Timer plays and how it scores.
Route Timer is an estimating game. It is on Slieve Muck, the seventh place on the Summit Ready map.
You build one game from each pair of game chapters. Route Timer is paired with Listen Out, so you build one of those two.
First you build Route Timer exactly as it is in Summit Ready. Then, in stage 5, you change it into an estimating game on your own topic.
A round has 5 [[legs|0]]. A leg is one part of a walk, such as Carrick Little to Slieve Binnian.
Each leg shows a photo on the left. On the right are the leg's distance in kilometres and its climb in metres.
Under the photo is a [[slider|2]] that runs from 0 to 4 hours. You drag it to your best guess of how long the leg takes. Your guess shows under the slider, such as **Your guess: 1 hour 55 minutes**.
The slider jumps in steps of 5 minutes, because nobody plans a walk to the exact minute.
When you are happy with your guess, you click **Lock in my time**. The game works out the time with [[Naismith's rule|1]], which walkers use to plan a day out.
Naismith's rule allows 12 minutes for every kilometre, plus 1 minute for every 10 metres of climb. The white box on the right shows the rule all the time.
After you lock in your time, the game shows its working. Under the slider, a bar shows 2 markers: your avatar at your guess, and a chequered flag at the Naismith time.
Your points depend on how far out your guess is:
10 minutes out or less scores 20 points, and the game says **Spot on.** 20 minutes out or less scores 12 points, and it says **Close.**
30 minutes out or less scores 5 points, and it says **A bit out.**
More than 30 minutes out scores 0 points, and the game says your guess was too far out.
A guess that scores 12 points or more turns the result message green and plays the right sound. Any other guess turns it red and plays the wrong sound.
After each leg, **Next leg** appears. After the 5th leg, the button says **See my score**, and it opens the Round over box.
The best score is 5 legs at 20 points each, which is 100 points. The flag on Slieve Muck gets a tick on the map.

box.title: Why real walkers add more time

blocks.p: Naismith's rule is for a fit walker on a good path in good weather. Real walkers add time for rests, rough ground, bad weather and a heavy rucksack.
The distances and climbs in Route Timer are rounded for practice. A real plan uses the exact figures from a map.

words: leg
One part of a walk, from one place to another. A round of Route Timer has 5 legs.
Naismith's rule
A rule walkers use to plan: 12 minutes for every kilometre, plus 1 minute for every 10 metres of climb.
slider
A control with a handle that you drag along a line to pick a number. In the Toolbox, a slider is called a TrackBar.
bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
property
A named value that an object carries, such as `Distance` on a RouteLeg. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read the value and change it.
constructor
A method with the same name as its class. It runs once, when code makes a new object with `new`.
static
A method marked `static` belongs to the class itself. You call it on the class name, as in `RouteLeg.LoadAll()`.
List
A list that grows as you add to it. `List<RouteLeg>` is a list that holds RouteLeg objects.
continue
Inside a loop, `continue` skips the rest of this turn of the loop. The loop goes straight on to its next turn.
double
A number that can have a decimal point, such as 4.5. An `int` can only hold a whole number.
Convert.ToDouble
Turns text such as `"4.5"` into the number 4.5.
Convert.ToInt32
Turns text, or a number with a decimal point, into a whole number.
lightning bolt
The button at the top of the Properties window that shows a control's events in place of its properties.
field
A variable written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the form can use it, and it keeps its value until the window closes.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `int[]` is an array of whole numbers.
panel
A control that holds other controls. `pnlBar` holds the bar and its 2 markers.
Scroll
The event a slider has when the player drags its handle.
whole-number division
`/` between two whole numbers drops anything after the decimal point. `115 / 60` is 1, not 1.9.
remainder
`%` gives what is left over after whole-number division. `115 % 60` is 55.
return
`return` hands a value back to the code that called the method, and stops the method.
Math.Round
Rounds a number to the nearest whole number, so 44.4 becomes 44.
Math.Abs
Gives a number without its minus sign, so -12 becomes 12. Route Timer uses it to find how far out a guess is, whichever side it misses on.
colour from red, green and blue
`Color.FromArgb(62, 142, 65)` mixes a colour from red, green and blue. Each number is from 0 to 255.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a button.
handler
The method that runs when an event happens. `btnLock_Click` is the handler for a click on **Lock in my time**.
AddRange
`AddRange` adds every item from one list to the end of another list, in one go.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet. Often it means a method you have not written yet.

box.title: If a file is missing or broken

blocks.p: Route Timer never crashes because a file is missing. This is what you see instead.
If `routes.txt` is missing, or has fewer than 5 good lines, a message box says **Route Timer needs 5 legs in Data\routes.txt, each with 5 parts.**
If a line of `routes.txt` does not have exactly 5 parts, Route Timer skips that line.
If a photo is missing, the space for the photo stays empty, and the game carries on.
If a sound is missing, that moment is silent, and the game carries on.
To put a missing file back, you download the [[zip file|4]] again and paste its folders into bin\Debug. When Windows asks about the files you already have, you click **Skip these files**.
Skipping keeps every file you already have, including any file you changed. Only the missing files are copied in.

code.title: RouteLeg.cs: the RouteLeg class
code.why: You type the 5 properties, and the 5 lines that put a value into each one, because they are new. The rest reads a file the same way as `LoadAll` in chapter 3, so it comes in the copy.
partLines: The class and its 5 properties

`class RouteLeg` starts the class. Each property holds one part of a line of `routes.txt`. `Distance` is a `double`, because a distance can be 4.5 kilometres. `Climb` is an `int`, because the climb is always whole metres.
The constructor

This part is the constructor. It runs when code writes `new RouteLeg(parts)`. `parts` is one line of `routes.txt`, already cut into 5 pieces at each bar. `Convert.ToDouble` turns the text `"4.5"` into the number 4.5. `Convert.ToInt32` turns the text `"600"` into the whole number 600.
The start of LoadAll

`static` means that you call LoadAll on the class itself, as `RouteLeg.LoadAll()`. LoadAll starts with an empty list. `Files.Data` from chapter 2 gives the full path of `routes.txt`. If `routes.txt` is not there, LoadAll hands back the empty list, so the game shows a message and does not crash.
Read every line

The loop goes round once for each line of `routes.txt`. `Split('|')` cuts each line at each bar. If a line does not have exactly 5 parts, `continue` skips it. Every good line becomes a new RouteLeg on the end of the list.
Close the file and hand back the list
`reader.Close()` closes `routes.txt`, so that other programs can open it again. `return legs;` hands the full list back to the code that called LoadAll.

screens.title: Type btnLock_Click, which works out the Naismith time and marks the guess

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, **Lock in my time** works out the Naismith time, shows the working and scores the guess.
This is the heart of Route Timer. Read the rule in words first, then see how each line of code follows it.

code.title: Naismith's rule, in words
code.text:
time for the distance  =  distance in kilometres × 12
time for the climb     =  metres of climb ÷ 10
Naismith time          =  time for the distance + time for the climb
how far out            =  the gap between your guess and the Naismith time
partLines: The distance
A walker covers 1 kilometre in 12 minutes on the flat. So the distance in kilometres, times 12, is the minutes of walking.
The climb
Every 10 metres of climb adds 1 minute. So the metres of climb, divided by 10, is the extra minutes.
The total
The 2 times added together give the Naismith time for the leg.
How far out
The gap is always counted as a number of minutes above 0, whether the guess is too long or too short.

box.title: Carrick Little to Slieve Binnian, worked through

blocks.p: The leg is 4.5 kilometres, with 600 metres of climb.
Time for the distance: 4.5 × 12 is 54 minutes. Time for the climb: 600 ÷ 10 is 60 minutes.
Naismith time: 54 + 60 is 114 minutes, which is 1 hour 54 minutes.
A guess of 1 hour 40 minutes is 100 minutes. The gap is 14 minutes, so the guess scores 12 points.
The code follows the rule line by line. The distance is a `double`, so `Math.Round` rounds the walking time to whole minutes, and `Convert.ToInt32` keeps it as a whole number.
btnLock_Click is long, so it comes in 3 pieces. Type them one after the other, in the same method.

code.title: btnLock_Click, first piece: the rule
partLines: This leg
`leg` is the leg on the screen now.
Time for the distance
`leg.Distance * 12` is the time for the distance. `Math.Round` rounds it to the nearest minute, and `Convert.ToInt32` turns it into an `int`. For 4.5 kilometres, `walk` is 54.
Time for the climb
`leg.Climb / 10` is the time for the climb. Both are whole numbers, so it is whole-number division. For 600 metres, `climb` is 60.
The Naismith time
`answer` is the Naismith time: 54 + 60, which is 114.
How far out
`guess` is the number the slider is on. `Math.Abs` takes off any minus sign, so `diff` is how far out the guess is, whichever side it misses on.
The points
LegPoints turns `diff` into the points for this leg.

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you have chosen your own formula and its data, and 2 more things to change.
Your own game keeps the Route Timer code, but uses your own topic. Any topic where a formula turns 2 numbers into one answer works.
Home economics: cooking time for a joint of meat, such as 20 minutes for every 500 grams, plus 20 minutes.
Physics: stopping distance, as thinking distance plus braking distance, from a car's speed.
Geography: travel time for a journey by bus, from its distance and its number of stops.

Change at least 2 more things as well, so that your game plays differently from Route Timer. For example, change the bands (how close a guess must be), the points, the number of rounds or the slider's range.

glossary: leg
One part of a walk, from one place to another. A round of Route Timer has 5 legs.
Naismith's rule
A rule walkers use to plan: 12 minutes for every kilometre, plus 1 minute for every 10 metres of climb.
slider
A control with a handle that you drag along a line to pick a number. In the Toolbox, a slider is called a TrackBar.
bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
property
A named value that an object carries, such as `Distance` on a RouteLeg. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read the value and change it.
constructor
A method with the same name as its class. It runs once, when code makes a new object with `new`.
static
A method marked `static` belongs to the class itself. You call it on the class name, as in `RouteLeg.LoadAll()`.
List
A list that grows as you add to it. `List<RouteLeg>` is a list that holds RouteLeg objects.
continue
Inside a loop, `continue` skips the rest of this turn of the loop. The loop goes straight on to its next turn.
double
A number that can have a decimal point, such as 4.5. An `int` can only hold a whole number.
Convert.ToDouble
Turns text such as `"4.5"` into the number 4.5.
Convert.ToInt32
Turns text, or a number with a decimal point, into a whole number.
lightning bolt
The button at the top of the Properties window that shows a control's events in place of its properties.
field
A variable written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the form can use it, and it keeps its value until the window closes.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `int[]` is an array of whole numbers.
panel
A control that holds other controls. `pnlBar` holds the bar and its 2 markers.
Scroll
The event a slider has when the player drags its handle.
whole-number division
`/` between two whole numbers drops anything after the decimal point. `115 / 60` is 1, not 1.9.
remainder
`%` gives what is left over after whole-number division. `115 % 60` is 55.
return
`return` hands a value back to the code that called the method, and stops the method.
Math.Round
Rounds a number to the nearest whole number, so 44.4 becomes 44.
Math.Abs
Gives a number without its minus sign, so -12 becomes 12. Route Timer uses it to find how far out a guess is, whichever side it misses on.
colour from red, green and blue
`Color.FromArgb(62, 142, 65)` mixes a colour from red, green and blue. Each number is from 0 to 255.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a button.
handler
The method that runs when an event happens. `btnLock_Click` is the handler for a click on **Lock in my time**.
AddRange
`AddRange` adds every item from one list to the end of another list, in one go.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet. Often it means a method you have not written yet.
